title: Lesson Planning Made Easy
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles argues that lesson planning has been turned into a tyrannous checklist of Ofsted buzzwords (differentiation, personalised resources, engaging starters, plenaries) that overwhelms teachers and distracts from learning. His move is to replace the checklist with one simple teaching sequence, See, Try, Apply, Secure, built by working backwards from what students do not yet know. He shows that this sequence automatically covers every buzzword: modelling makes success criteria explicit, pairs correct misconceptions, and repeated mini-plenaries replace the whole-class check. A maths example and a full Year 10 English lesson plan illustrate how altering the context in the Secure stage communicates high expectations without extra planning. The piece is an extract from The Slightly Awesome Teacher and treats simplicity as the route to sustainable, rigorous teaching.
points: Planning is reframed as simply making sure students are learning, starting from the success criteria and working back from the endpoint.
The See, Try, Apply, Secure sequence is claimed to satisfy differentiation, engaging starters, plenaries and variety without separate planning for each.
The Secure stage tests understanding of the concept by altering the context, which is where high expectations are actually communicated.
The model chosen at the start (for example a richer mnemonic than AFOREST) sets the ceiling of expectation for the whole lesson.
Choosing two or three student exemplars from a few books gives marking a purpose and keeps the workload sustainable.
quotes: The skills and knowledge required for a student to gain an A or A*, or an 8 or 9 grade have been fought over by senior examiners who are passionate about your subject. To start here is not to sell out to the system, but to make the system work for your students.
What you mustn’t do is go out and find something engaging to grip their attention – I’ve lost count of the starters I’ve seen that have nothing to do with the learning in the lesson.

Anyone with a good memory can follow a method in a single lesson and achieve apparent mastery. But once a problem that looks slightly different arrives, such students panic – the method no longer suffices.
The key to the secure stage is finding ways to test your students’ understanding of the concept, rather than just what has happened in the lesson. To do this, you want to alter the context.
Instead I am offering simplicity. Simplicity is always sustainable. It is also precise, and will consequently deliver high expectations, whatever you are teaching.
